body_markdown:
When an artist dies, their music rights do not automatically pass to the person managing their legacy, nor does the family necessarily inherit the entire catalog. What transfers depends on what the artist owned, the contracts they signed and the estate-planning documents they left behind.


In the United States, copyright can pass under a will or through intestate succession. Rights already held in a trust or company follow a different path. Royalty payments, licensing authority and federal copyright termination interests also require separate analysis.


For labels, publishers, managers and heirs, the central task is to establish **what passes, to whom and who can act during the transition** . This guide addresses U.S. law; individual estates require advice on applicable state law and any international holdings.


## Which music rights can an artist’s estate inherit?


An estate can administer only the interests the artist actually held at death. Being the performer, songwriter or public face of a release does not establish ownership of every associated asset.


Start by separating the song from the recording. A songwriter may own a share of the composition while a label owns the master. Our guide to[composition ownership](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/composition-copyright-what-songwriters-actually-own) explains that underlying distinction.

Possession of session files, original tapes or a hard drive does not, by itself, establish copyright ownership. Likewise, a royalty statement can prove a payment relationship without proving ownership of the underlying work.


The inventory of music rights should therefore identify ownership, income entitlements and approval powers as separate fields, rather than treating them as one asset.


## How copyright passes through a will, probate or a trust


### A will directs succession, but administration still matters


[Section 201(d)(1) of the Copyright Act](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/201) expressly allows copyright to be bequeathed by will or to pass as personal property under intestate succession law.


A will might leave a catalog to a spouse, divide it among children or place it in a testamentary trust. It cannot transfer a copyright the artist previously sold. A gift also remains subject to applicable estate administration, creditor claims and other legal obligations.


If there is no valid will, state intestacy rules determine who inherits. Those rules do not necessarily match the artist’s informal promises, management arrangements or family expectations.


During probate, the executor or administrator generally acts under authority granted by state law and the court. The precise timing of title vesting and the representative’s powers varies by jurisdiction, so an heir’s eventual economic interest should not be confused with present authority to sign agreements.


For counterparties acquiring or licensing music rights, the operative evidence may include court-issued letters, the will, relevant orders and documents establishing any completed distribution.


### A funded living trust follows its own ownership structure


If the artist validly transferred copyright into a living trust before death, the successor trustee generally administers it under the trust rather than through probate. Merely listing a catalog in an estate plan does not necessarily complete that transfer.


Confirm the assignment documents, trust provisions and successor trustee’s authority. Copyright transfers generally require a signed writing unless they occur by operation of law, so the ownership documentation matters.


A company creates another distinction. If an LLC owns the masters, the artist’s estate may inherit membership interests rather than the copyrights themselves. The company remains the rights holder, while its operating agreement determines who can manage it.


This distinction affects deal execution: an executor’s authority over estate assets does not automatically make that executor an authorized signatory for a separate company.


## Who can authorize licenses after the artist dies?


The person entitled to inherit music rights is not necessarily the person authorized to negotiate or execute a license today. Authority may sit with an executor, trustee, company manager or existing administrator, depending on the ownership structure and governing documents.


Before accepting an estate-side signature, establish both the chain of title and the signer’s capacity. A family spokesperson or longtime manager may understand the catalog without having legal authority to bind its owner.


Existing licenses also require review. Death does not automatically cancel every publishing, recording or synchronization agreement. Check survival provisions, termination clauses, assignment restrictions and approval requirements. Personal services and agency arrangements can raise different issues from completed copyright grants.


A new use may require approvals from several parties. An estate holding the composition cannot necessarily authorize the master, and a minority ownership interest does not establish exclusive control over every share.


For advertising or synchronization deals, confirm the[scope of the required music licenses](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/law-license-basics-how-modern-music-licenses-actually-work) separately from any estate consent to use the artist’s name, likeness or endorsement. Those permissions address different interests.


## Royalty payments need their own succession process


Changing ownership records does not automatically redirect every payment stream. Publishers, labels, distributors, collection societies and other payors maintain separate accounts and documentation requirements.


The estate should reconcile accrued but unpaid amounts, ongoing royalty entitlements and any balances affected by advances or recoupment. A stream that produces substantial usage may still generate little current cash if contractual deductions remain outstanding.


A beneficiary who inherits music rights should not assume that payment-account updates also establish ownership, licensing authority or entitlement to every category of income. Each conclusion needs its own supporting documents.


Depending on the payor, administration may involve a death certificate, evidence of representative authority, tax documentation, banking instructions and distribution or trust records. Requirements differ, so obtain them directly rather than relying on another organization’s process.


Keep songwriter, publisher, performer and master-owner accounts distinct. The same individual may have received income in several capacities, with different contractual or statutory rules governing each.


For valuation, separate gross historical receipts from the estate’s actual economic interest. Ownership percentages, administration fees, recoupment, contract duration and approval restrictions all affect what beneficiaries or a catalog buyer will receive. Avoid valuing the inheritance from headline royalty figures alone.


## How long does copyright last after death?


Inheriting music rights does not restart the copyright term. The estate receives the remaining protection attached to the work.


For many individually authored works created on or after January 1, 1978, U.S. copyright lasts for the author’s life plus 70 years. For qualifying joint works, the term generally runs for 70 years after the last surviving author’s death.


Other categories follow different rules. Works made for hire generally receive 95 years from publication or 120 years from creation, whichever ends first. Older works, anonymous or pseudonymous works and certain pre-1972 sound recordings require separate analysis. These distinctions appear in the Copyright Act’s[duration provisions](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/302) and related sections.


Catalog teams should calculate duration work by work, not apply one date to an artist’s entire output. A composition and its recording can have different terms, and foreign protection may end on a different schedule.


Unreleased material also deserves a publication-history review before anyone announces a release, licenses an archive or estimates its remaining protection.


## Copyright termination can follow different inheritance rules


### The inherited copyright and the termination interest are not the same


Federal termination law creates an important exception to ordinary estate planning. Certain prior copyright grants can be terminated under statutory conditions, potentially returning rights that the artist had transferred away.


For qualifying grants executed by an author on or after January 1, 1978,[Section 203](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/203) provides the relevant framework. It excludes works made for hire and grants made by will. Earlier grants may fall under Section 304 instead.


When the author has died, Section 203 allocates the termination interest among specified statutory successors. It establishes shares for a surviving spouse, children and grandchildren. If none of those survives, the statute provides for the author’s executor, administrator, personal representative or trustee.


Consequently, music rights received under a will and interests arising through copyright termination may belong to different people. A beneficiary named in the will cannot assume that the same document controls the statutory termination interest.


### Termination requires a separate timeline and authority review


Termination is not automatic upon death. It requires an eligible grant, the proper parties and compliance with formal notice requirements.


Under Section 203, the termination window generally opens 35 years after execution, with special timing rules for grants covering publication. Notice must generally be served between two and ten years before the effective termination date, and a copy must be recorded with the Copyright Office before that date.


Required ownership thresholds and signatures depend on the circumstances. Neither a single heir’s request nor an executor’s general probate appointment necessarily resolves those requirements.


An audit of music rights should therefore include a separate termination calendar identifying grant dates, signatories, possible effective dates and statutory successors. Death can occur while a notice period is already running, making early review particularly important.


## A hypothetical estate shows why the distinctions matter


Suppose a deceased singer-songwriter retained half of several compositions, assigned other songs to a publisher and owned an LLC holding independently released masters. A major label owns the recordings from an earlier album, but the artist remained entitled to contractual royalties.


The will leaves the residue of the estate to two children. A surviving spouse also has interests that require review under applicable state law and federal termination provisions.


The children do not automatically receive the major label’s masters. They may inherit the artist’s contractual royalty entitlement, the retained composition interests and the LLC membership interest, subject to administration and the governing documents.


The publisher’s previously acquired rights do not disappear merely because the songwriter died. Any potential termination of those grants requires separate statutory analysis. Meanwhile, the LLC’s authorized manager, not necessarily either child, may control master licensing.


This example illustrates why transferring music rights is not one transaction. Copyright title, company control, royalty administration and termination interests each require their own succession analysis and documentation.


## Build an estate handoff file before approving new deals


A usable handoff file should let a licensing team trace each asset from the artist’s ownership to the person or entity now authorized to act. It should also distinguish confirmed facts from unresolved claims.


Organize the review around these records:


-


**Catalog inventory:** Titles, alternate titles, ISRCs, ISWCs, ownership shares and relevant release or publication information.


-


**Ownership evidence:** Copyright registrations, assignments, writer split agreements and documents supporting any work-made-for-hire position.


-


**Contract file:** Recording, publishing, administration, distribution and licensing agreements, including amendments and royalty schedules.


-


**Succession authority:** Relevant wills, trust documents, court-issued letters, distribution instruments and company governance records.


-


**Payment records:** Payor contacts, account identifiers, statements, recoupment balances and pending amounts.


-


**Risk calendar:** Contract deadlines, potential termination windows, disputes and unresolved approval requirements.


For every asset, record who owns it, who receives income and who can sign. That simple separation prevents a royalty beneficiary from being mistaken for a licensing representative.


Documentation supporting the transfer of music rights should also be evaluated for Copyright Office recordation. The Office’s[recordation guidance](https://www.copyright.gov/recordation/) explains its process for transfers and other documents pertaining to copyright. Recordation can support the public ownership record, but it does not cure a defective transfer or replace probate analysis.


Keep disputed shares visibly marked. A clearance team should not treat an unresolved estate claim as established ownership simply because a release or advertising deadline is approaching.


## Frequently asked questions


**Do music rights automatically go to an artist’s spouse?** Not necessarily. Ownership, a valid will, state intestacy law, trust arrangements and spousal protections all matter. Federal copyright termination rules have their own succession provisions, which must be analyzed separately from ordinary inheritance.


**Can an executor license the catalog before the estate closes?** Potentially, if the executor has the necessary authority and the proposed transaction falls within it. State law, court orders, contractual restrictions and co-owner interests may limit that power. Counterparties should verify authority rather than rely on the executor’s title alone.


**Does inheriting royalties mean inheriting copyright?** No. A beneficiary may receive contractual royalty income while a label or publisher continues to own the copyright. Conversely, inherited copyright can remain subject to administration agreements, existing licenses or payment arrangements that constrain immediate income.


**Can heirs sell the catalog?** They may be able to sell interests they own or authorize a sale through the appropriate fiduciary. They cannot convey another owner’s share or disregard applicable restrictions. Buyers should review chain of title, signing authority, existing encumbrances and potential statutory termination exposure.


**Do unreleased songs pass through the estate?** Copyright in original music generally arises when it is fixed, not when it is released or registered. If the artist owned the relevant copyright at death, that interest can pass through succession. Ownership of recordings, contributions from collaborators and contractual restrictions still need review.


## Start with ownership and authority, not the family tree


Before distributing income, approving a synchronization request or marketing a catalog for sale, commission a coordinated review by estate counsel and music copyright counsel.


The first deliverable should be an asset-by-asset schedule identifying the owner, authorized signatory, income recipient and unresolved issues. That gives heirs and commercial partners a reliable basis for decisions without assuming that inheritance, control and payment rights are interchangeable.
